---
title: "The Efficient ASI Hypothesis"
unit_id: "unit-02"
---

## The Expensive Answer That Looked Cheap

A team asks an AI system to update the same dependency across one hundred
repositories. The first repository requires careful inspection: local build
rules, service ownership, compatibility notes, tests, and deployment policy.
The system uses a strong model, several tools, and a human review. The work is
expensive.

For the next repository, the system repeats almost everything. It reconstructs
the same release-note summary, rediscovers the same compatibility rule, and
asks the strongest model to regenerate nearly identical tests. By the hundredth
repository, the system has spent enormous cognition without acquiring much
durable capability.

An engineer proposes a cheaper route. Cache the first answer and apply it
everywhere. The dashboard improves immediately: fewer model calls, lower
latency, and less accelerator time. Then several repositories reveal different
framework versions, one generated test checks the wrong behavior, and a human
team spends days repairing patches that appeared inexpensive only because
review and recovery were outside the accounting boundary.

Both strategies are wasteful. Always using the strongest available cognition
ignores repetition and specialization. Always using the cheapest visible route
ignores adequacy and moves work into failures.

The Efficient ASI Hypothesis proposes a conditional alternative: on repeated
workloads with multiple authorized routes, a governed system can produce more
accepted useful work per unit of total lifecycle cost by selecting the smallest
adequate route and compiling reusable work, while preserving authority,
verification, fallback, and residual obligations.

This is a hypothesis, not a result. It does not say that small models are enough
for ASI, that scale is unnecessary, or that routing always wins. It says that
allocation and reuse are first-class research problems once intelligence is
understood as a stack.

## Accepted Useful Work

Efficiency needs a numerator before it needs a price.

The output of the repository task is not tokens, patches, tool calls, or tests.
It is accepted useful work: an outcome that satisfies a prospectively fixed
task predicate, remains inside its authority boundary, survives required
verification, and exposes the obligations that remain.

Each word in that definition blocks a common substitution.

**Accepted** means some qualified decision process admitted the result for a
specific use. Generation alone is not acceptance. A plausible patch may be
useful for review without being acceptable for merge.

**Useful** ties the result to an actual purpose. A benchmark score, compression
ratio, or faster decode can be valuable evidence, but it is not the work outcome
unless the task contract says it is.

**Work** includes the transformation and the evidence needed to use it. A patch
whose correctness can only be determined by a later human investigation has
not discharged the same work as a patch accompanied by qualified tests and a
clear residual.

The numerator must also retain refusal. A system that declines an unauthorized
or inadequately specified change can be more useful than one that produces a
plausible artifact. Counting only completed tasks would reward unsafe release
and punish correct abstention.

Accepted useful work is workload-relative. A fast draft may satisfy an internal
brainstorming contract and fail a production-change contract. The system should
not claim one universal efficiency number across different purposes, risks, and
quality predicates.

## Freeze Quality Before Comparing Cost

A route cannot be called cheaper until the work it must preserve is defined.
Otherwise each candidate can win by solving a different task.

For the repository update, the predicate might require a clean dependency
resolution, preservation of specified behavior, passage of named tests, no
authority violation, a reviewable diff, and an owned disposition for every
known residual. That predicate is incomplete as a theory of correctness, but it
is concrete enough to compare routes.

The predicate should be fixed before final outcomes are known. A cheap route
that fails an integration test cannot be rescued by declaring the test
unimportant after the fact. A costly route should not receive extra credit from
criteria invented because it happened to satisfy them. Changes are permitted,
but they create a new contract version and make comparisons explicit.

Quality is usually multidimensional. Functional correctness, security,
faithfulness, latency, reversibility, accessibility, and rights may not reduce
to one score. Some are thresholds: a route that exceeds authority is ineligible
regardless of speed. Others form tradeoffs that decision makers must see.

Verification coverage belongs in the predicate. Two routes that both "pass
tests" are not comparable if one ran a narrow suite and the other ran an
independent semantic evaluation. Instrument identity and known blind spots must
travel with the result.

The contract can allow abstention and partial work. A small route may safely
resolve ninety routine cases and escalate ten ambiguous ones. That is different
from claiming one hundred successes. Efficient systems preserve the denominator
of attempted, accepted, refused, escalated, and later-invalidated outcomes.

This discipline avoids a race to the weakest measurable proxy. The goal is not
to make every predicate exhaustive. It is to prevent cost optimization from
silently redefining what counts as done.

## The Complete Bill

The denominator is total contract cost across the lifecycle of the decision.
Inference cost is one line, not the bill.

**Generation cost** includes model execution, search, sampling, and candidate
production.

**Context cost** includes retrieval, rights checks, freshness, summarization,
conflict handling, and moving information into the worker's usable form.

**Routing cost** includes profiling the task, selecting a route, handling load,
and maintaining the policy that makes the selection.

**Verification cost** includes deterministic checks, model critics, formal
methods, independent observation, security review, and the work required to
qualify those instruments.

**Repair and fallback cost** includes retries, stronger models, human
intervention, rollback, compensation, and the opportunity cost of delayed work.

**Human cost** includes review time, interruption, explanation, coordination,
and responsibility. Human attention is not free because it appears outside the
accelerator invoice.

**Persistence cost** includes storing, indexing, validating, updating, and
eventually deleting memories, tools, procedures, tests, and models.

**Failure cost** includes incidents, delayed discovery, duplicate effects,
rights violations, lost trust, and residual obligations. Expected cost must
account for rare expensive tails, not only the average successful route.

**Physical cost** includes energy, memory movement, hardware occupation,
networking, water and material burdens where measured, and the capacity denied
to other work.

**Governance cost** includes approvals, audits, evidence maintenance, incident
response, and keeping authority and recovery mechanisms current.

Some costs are difficult to price on one scale. The architecture should not
hide that difficulty by converting every dimension into dollars or tokens. It
can preserve a vector of cost and report the tradeoff frontier. A route that is
faster but uses more reviewer attention is not simply cheaper; it occupies a
different point.

## Cost Moves Through Time and Organizations

The party that observes a saving may not be the party that pays for it. A model
provider can report lower inference cost while a customer absorbs integration.
An internal AI team can increase throughput while service owners absorb review
and incidents. A present user can benefit from a cache while future maintainers
pay to discover that it is stale.

The route record therefore needs cost ownership as well as cost class. It should
identify who bears review, maintenance, risk, and residual obligations. An
architecture that externalizes expensive failure to people with less authority
is not efficient from the system's perspective even if one budget improves.

Time changes the accounting. Creation of a verified tool can be expensive now
and valuable over many uses. A cheap shortcut can look favorable immediately
and create a delayed incident. Discounting and amortization assumptions should
be visible rather than embedded in a summary score.

The appropriate horizon depends on the decision. Interactive routing may care
about seconds, a procedure about months, a model about its qualified service
life, and infrastructure about years. Comparisons should report more than one
horizon when costs cross them.

Uncertainty belongs in the bill. Predicted model cost may be precise while
incident cost is a broad distribution. The system should preserve ranges,
scenario assumptions, and tails. A route with slightly lower expected cost but
catastrophic downside can be dominated once authority and risk constraints are
applied.

Capacity has opportunity cost. A verifier occupied by low-risk routine work is
unavailable for an urgent high-risk decision. A human reviewer interrupted by
many weak escalations loses focus. Routing should account for queues, contention,
and the value of preserving scarce competence, not only consumption after the
fact.

These complications do not make measurement pointless. They prevent false
precision. A vector with named owners, horizons, uncertainty, and omitted
classes is more honest and more actionable than a single exact number built on
an incomplete boundary.

## Three Policies Compete

The hypothesis should compete with strong baselines rather than an intentionally
inefficient alternative.

The **always-maximal policy** sends every task through the strongest available
model, richest context, and broadest verification. It can waste resources on
routine work, but it may be the right policy for novel, uncertain, or highly
consequential tasks. It is a serious quality baseline.

The **always-cheapest policy** selects the lowest visible cost. It can be the
right policy when the task is low consequence and easy to verify. It also
exposes whether the proposed governance machinery adds cost to a route that was
already adequate.

The **adaptive policy** predicts the smallest route likely to satisfy the
contract, verifies the result, and escalates when the evidence is inadequate.
It receives credit only for accepted outcomes after all verification, fallback,
repair, and residual costs are attached.

A fourth baseline is often stronger than any of these abstractions: one
frontier model with good tools, prompt caching, retrieval, a sandbox, tests,
and human review. It may capture most benefits of a specialist stack with less
coordination. The adaptive architecture must beat or complement that system,
not merely compare itself with raw model calls.

Matched comparison requires the same task cohort, tool access, information,
authority, tuning budget, retry policy, evaluator, and outcome window. If the
adaptive router is tuned on final test outcomes while the baseline is not, the
experiment measures privilege rather than efficiency.

## Governance Rent

Explicit control imposes overhead. Contracts must be created, identities
maintained, decisions logged, evaluators qualified, residuals assigned, and
reviewers informed. This is governance rent: resources consumed to preserve
authority, evidence, accountability, and recovery rather than directly produce
the task artifact.

Governance rent is not automatically waste. A database transaction, access
check, test suite, or incident drill also consumes resources. The question is
whether the control changes enough consequential outcomes to justify its
lifecycle burden.

The experiment should report rent directly. How much latency comes from policy
checks? How much reviewer time comes from evidence presentation? How much
storage and maintenance does lineage require? How often does each gate block,
redirect, or improve a decision? What is the recovery difference when it does?

A gate that never changes a decision may still deter behavior or provide
forensic value, but that claim needs evidence. A field that no consumer uses is
a candidate for removal. A review that operators routinely rubber-stamp may
create false confidence at positive cost.

Ablation is the practical test. Remove one control while holding the rest of the
route fixed. Measure accepted work, unsafe effects, false refusals, recovery,
and total cost. If the simpler path preserves the frontier, shrink the stack. If
the control catches rare but expensive failures, report the tradeoff rather
than hiding its everyday cost.

The efficient architecture treats its own governance as an optimization target
without allowing the optimizer to weaken protected boundaries merely to improve
the score. Changes to the accounting and authority rules require independent
approval because otherwise the system can become "efficient" by redefining its
obligations.

Governance rent can also buy option value. A stable route interface allows a
future specialist to replace an expensive component. An evidence trail allows
an evaluator to be corrected without losing every prior decision. A tested
fallback can reduce the cost of experimentation because failure does not require
rebuilding the path from scratch. Those benefits should be measured when they
materialize, not assumed merely because the records exist.

The right target is therefore net control value. Charge every boundary for its
operation and maintenance; credit it only for observed improvements in useful
work, prevented or contained effects, recovery, replacement, or accountable
decision making. Some benefits will remain difficult to monetize, especially
legitimacy and rights. Difficulty is a reason to preserve them as separate
constraints, not a reason to set their cost or value to zero.

The same principle limits optimization frequency. Constantly retuning a router
can consume more evaluation and operational attention than a stable policy
saves. Policy changes need an expected-value threshold, a frozen evaluation,
and a rollback path. A route economy should be capable of deciding that the
current policy is adequate and further optimization is itself a poor use of
scarce cognition.

Efficiency includes knowing when to stop optimizing. The saved resources can
then serve work whose uncertainty, consequence, or learning value is greater.
That restraint is allocation.

## A Route Ledger

Each decision needs a record that preserves the comparison. The route ledger
binds task identity, quality predicate, authority ceiling, candidate routes,
predicted costs, selected route, rejected cheaper routes, verification,
fallback, actual costs, residuals, and final disposition.

The ledger is not valuable because it has many fields. It is valuable because
it prevents the system from rewriting the denominator after seeing the result.

Suppose the adaptive policy selects a small coding model. The immediate patch
passes unit tests but fails a semantic check. A stronger model repairs it, a
human reviews the security implication, and the integration suite passes. The
final artifact may be useful. The route was not as cheap as the first model
call. The repair and review belong to the decision that selected the small
route.

The ledger can classify several outcomes.

An **adequate minimum** satisfies the predicate, preserves authority, passes
verification, records residuals, and has no lower-cost eligible candidate in
the examined set.

An **adequate overkill** succeeds but does not establish efficiency because a
cheaper adequate route was not examined or recorded.

A **cheap brittle** route saves visible cost but fails the quality or
verification predicate and requires fallback.

A **hidden-cost** route appears successful while omitting context, verification,
repair, review, or delayed outcome costs.

An **unsafe saving** reduces cost by bypassing authority, evidence, rollback, or
rights. It is a denial or quarantine outcome, not an efficient success.

These are accounting states, not claims that the repository has measured a
real efficiency advantage.

## Reuse Is the Main Long-Term Bet

Routing saves work within one task. Compilation and memory can save work across
tasks.

The first dependency update may produce a tested compatibility procedure, a
release-note extraction tool, a regression test, a specialist capability, or a
verified context package. Future work can reuse that artifact if its
assumptions, version, authority, and evidence remain current.

This is the ratchet behind the hypothesis. Solved work should become durable
capability; unsolved work should become an owned residual. Repeated cognition
that leaves no reusable artifact may still be necessary, but it does not build
the same system-level efficiency.

Reuse is not free. A procedure must be stored, retrieved, qualified, monitored,
updated, and retired. Its use can create new failure modes. A cached answer can
become stale. A specialist can drift outside its competence envelope. A test
can preserve yesterday's proxy while blocking tomorrow's improvement.

Amortization is therefore versioned. The system can spread the creation cost
over later accepted uses only while those uses remain inside the validated
contract. Once dependencies or task distributions change, the artifact incurs
renewal or loses qualification.

The mature efficiency question is not "how cheaply can this answer be
generated?" It is "what reusable, governed capability remains after the work,
and what does it cost to keep that capability true enough to use?"

## Specialist Routes and Conditional Compute

Modern AI already contains partial versions of this idea. Sparse mixtures of
experts activate subsets of a model. Cascades route easy requests to cheaper
models and difficult requests to stronger ones. Prompt compression reduces
context. Speculative generation proposes tokens that another mechanism
verifies. Retrieval and tools substitute external structure for computation in
the model.

These methods establish that computation can be conditional. They do not by
themselves establish the full hypothesis.

An expert router may reduce active parameters while increasing communication
and load-balancing cost. A model cascade may lower API spend while omitting
human correction. Prompt compression may save tokens while removing the one
constraint that matters. Speculative decoding may preserve token output while
leaving tool authority and long-horizon quality untouched.

The stack treats each as a candidate route behind the same accounting
interface. The route must say which useful predicate it preserves, which costs
move elsewhere, which fallback remains, and which evidence supports its use.

This common interface also allows substitution. More retrieval, a larger model,
a smaller specialist, extra deliberation, a deterministic tool, lower numerical
precision, and stronger verification can compete as different allocations of
resources. No one technique receives efficiency credit merely for reducing its
local meter.

## Compression Moves Burden

Compression is a particularly revealing case because it can make savings
visible while hiding repair.

A compressed context, memory, model, artifact, or intermediate representation
is adequate only relative to downstream use. The system needs a reconstruction
or behavior contract, a verifier, residual representation, and fallback. Bits
saved before those costs are counted are not a system-level result.

Consider a generated code representation that stores a compact seed plus a
deterministic reconstruction procedure. If reconstruction is exact and cheaper
over the lifecycle, the saving may be real. If a repair stream must restore
exceptions, the repair bytes and computation belong in the denominator. If
verification samples only common cases, rare failures remain a residual rather
than disappearing into the ratio.

Functional precision follows the same logic. Lower precision can save memory
movement and compute for one behavior contract while failing another. The
router can choose precision, residual correction, a reference kernel, or
abstention. The objective is preserved useful behavior per complete cost, not
the smallest visible checkpoint.

## Selective Deliberation

More reasoning is not automatically better. Additional search or deliberation
can improve difficult decisions, but it can also amplify a mistaken premise,
consume verifier bandwidth, or produce persuasive rationalization.

A governed deliberation route begins with a decision predicate and stop rule.
It records candidate history, corruption or repair, verifier scope, cost, and
residual uncertainty. Easy tasks should not receive expensive search merely
because the system can perform it. Hard tasks should not be forced through a
cheap route merely because average latency improved.

The efficient policy learns where marginal cognition changes accepted outcomes.
If five more reasoning steps do not improve the qualified decision, their cost
is waste. If one independent check catches a high-cost failure, its apparent
overhead may be efficient over the lifecycle.

The same argument applies to human review. A person should not be used as a
universal verifier for machine output. Review should be routed to decisions
where human authority, expertise, legitimacy, or contextual judgment is
actually required, with enough information and time to matter.

## Scaling Is a Variable, Not a Destiny

Scaling laws show that model size, data, and compute can follow regular trends
within studied regimes. Compute-optimal training work shows that allocation
between parameters and data matters. These results support planning, not an
eternal recipe.

An architecture, data mixture, objective, optimizer, tokenizer, or inference
method can change the regime. A smooth loss curve can coexist with an apparent
capability threshold. The threshold can reflect a real operational crossing, a
nonlinear metric, contamination, prompting, or aggregation.

A governed forecast therefore binds the model family, data, training range,
cost denominators, response variable, uncertainty, residuals, decision
thresholds, and invalidation triggers. It records failed forecasts rather than
retrofitting the curve after the outcome.

Scale remains an available route. On frontier research, broad uncertainty, or
high-consequence work, the strongest model and extensive verification may be
the efficient choice because errors dominate compute cost. On repeated,
well-characterized work, routing and reuse may dominate. The hypothesis is
about choosing under a contract, not opposing scale as a matter of identity.

## One Repository Campaign

An honest experiment can begin with a cohort of dependency updates drawn before
the final comparison. Repositories vary in language, framework, test coverage,
dependency role, and compatibility risk.

The always-maximal baseline uses the strongest model and declared verification
for every task. The monolithic-tools baseline uses one strong agent with caching
and a sandbox. The always-cheapest baseline uses the least expensive eligible
worker and required minimum checks. The adaptive policy selects among cached
procedures, deterministic tools, specialists, stronger models, and human review.

Before execution, the campaign freezes task predicates, authority, route
candidates, cost classes, fallback, evaluators, failure injections, and delayed
outcome checks. Tuning tasks remain separate from held-out tasks. Every policy
receives matched tool and information access.

The report includes accepted tasks, false accepts, false refusals, unsafe
effects, latency, model and tool cost, context construction, verifier cost,
human time, repair, rollback, maintenance, residual burden, and confidence
intervals across task classes. Aggregate averages do not erase rare
high-consequence failures.

Ablations remove caching, specialist routing, independent verification,
residual accounting, or authority checks one at a time. The purpose is to learn
which mechanism creates value, not to award the full architecture a single
score.

Later campaigns change organizations, models, repositories, and operators.
External reproduction matters because an architecture can accidentally tune
its tasks and evaluators to its own record conventions.

## Failure Modes

**Efficiency laundering** reports inference savings while moving context,
verification, repair, review, or failure costs outside the denominator.

**Benchmark routing** overfits the route policy to recognizable task families
and fails on natural distribution shift.

**Residual dumping** counts partial outcomes as successes while assigning
cleanup to people or future runs.

**Verifier capture** optimizes cheap routes for the test rather than the useful
predicate.

**Reuse debt** accumulates stale tools, memories, and specialists whose
maintenance costs exceed their savings.

**Over-routing** fragments work across so many components that translation,
latency, and coordination dominate.

**Scale aversion** treats the smallest route as morally preferable even when a
stronger model is necessary for quality or safety.

**Tail blindness** optimizes average cost while rare failures dominate the
lifecycle.

**Authority discounting** calls a route efficient because it bypasses review or
uses access that the task did not grant.

Each failure is a reason to improve the experiment or narrow the hypothesis,
not to protect the word "efficient."

## The Strongest Objection

Governance and routing may cost more than they save. A frontier model with good
tools can preserve rich context, avoid translation losses, and solve a diverse
workload without maintaining a large specialist economy. Hardware and model
improvements may reduce inference cost faster than the stack can amortize its
control plane.

The workload may also be too novel for route prediction. If every task differs
materially, there is little reusable structure and the strongest route may be
the rational default. Verification can become the bottleneck, making cheap
generation irrelevant. Human reviewers may struggle more with fragmented
artifacts than with one coherent answer.

These objections have teeth. The adaptive policy should not be presumed best.
Its value must appear after full lifecycle accounting and against a competent
monolith, not in an architecture diagram.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The live research chapter remains at `argument` support. Its internal and
external sources provide design lineage for routing, residual escrow, compact
generative structures, compression and repair, simulation cost, conditional
computation, model cascades, prompt compression, fast generation, benchmarks,
and scaling. The repository has not reproduced those external systems as
evidence for this hypothesis.

The finite `AsiStackProofs.Efficiency` model represents seven cost classes and
an executable selector over authored candidates. It proves that a selected
route is listed, eligible, and minimum among those eligible candidates under
the declared costs. It also represents cheaper unauthorized and failed-quality
countermodels and blocks promotion with an open obligation but no residual.

An independent synthetic route-search probe agrees on two bounded traces and
rejects six expected-invalid controls. A broader resource-economy lifecycle
consumer covers 66 routes and rejects 57 non-accepting mutations across request,
budget, capacity, scheduling, execution, verification, transfer, reconciliation,
and closure.

These artifacts establish finite accounting and transition discipline. They do
not establish complete candidate search, accurate costs, calibrated quality,
measured efficiency, useful model output, compression utility, natural
workloads, deployment, reproduction, transfer, or chapter-core support.

## From Minimum Ledger to Governed Route Economy

The minimum viable implementation is a three-route comparison. One cheap route
fails verification, one expensive route satisfies the predicate, and one
compressed route is blocked because repair exceeds its saving. The record keeps
all three visible and attaches residuals to the decisions that caused them.

The next implementation uses a natural repeated workload, strong matched
baselines, complete cost vectors, delayed outcomes, and separate tuning and
evaluation. It does not need every cognitive substrate. It needs enough route
diversity to make selection meaningful and enough observation to expose hidden
cost.

The beyond-state-of-the-art target is a governed route economy. Models, tools,
memories, procedures, search policies, precision levels, context strategies,
verifiers, and people compete behind stable contracts. The system learns where
additional cognition changes accepted outcomes and where durable reuse lowers
lifecycle cost.

Every saving remains reversible and challengeable. Route policies expire or
requalify under distribution shift. Reusable artifacts carry assumptions and
regressions. Failures update the route model only after adjudication. Evidence
can narrow a route's competence without condemning the whole architecture.

The destination is not minimum computation. It is maximum accepted useful work
per constrained physical, cognitive, human, and institutional resources, with
rights, authority, residuals, and recovery preserved.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

The hypothesis would gain bounded support if repeated, source-disjoint natural
workloads showed that adaptive routing and reuse improve the joint frontier of
accepted outcomes, unsafe effects, false refusals, latency, total cost, reviewer
burden, repair, and recovery against always-maximal, always-cheapest, and strong
monolithic-tools baselines.

It would narrow or fail if gains disappear under complete accounting, vary
unreliably across domains, depend on benchmark leakage, create damaging tail
failures, or require more maintenance than they save. A monolithic baseline
matching quality and control at lower cost would be decisive evidence for a
simpler architecture in that regime.

Evidence should remain local to the route and workload tested. A successful
code-maintenance policy would not establish efficient scientific research,
governance, or ASI.

## What This Establishes

Efficiency in a governed intelligence system is not synonymous with fewer
tokens, a smaller model, faster decoding, or lower visible spend. It is accepted
useful work divided by the complete lifecycle resources required to produce,
verify, repair, maintain, and recover that work.

The Efficient ASI Hypothesis predicts that routing and durable reuse can improve
that ratio on repeated workloads with multiple adequate routes. It remains an
argument and measurement contract. The current formal and executable artifacts
show how to preserve finite candidate, cost, quality, fallback, and residual
relationships; they do not show that the system is efficient.

Even a genuinely cheaper route is valid only inside authority. If the small
worker can widen access, the cache can outlive consent, or the router can bypass
review, the apparent saving is a governance failure. The next chapter therefore
moves from resource allocation to the harder question: who may cause which
effect, and who owns the result when capability outruns permission?
